title: How a reverse proxy handles a request
summary: One public entry point hides many private servers.

steps.n: The browser connects to the one public address, which belongs to the proxy rather than to any app server.
The proxy matches the host name and path against its configuration to pick a backend.
For a cacheable page the proxy first asks its cache, which may answer without bothering the app.
On a miss the proxy opens or reuses a connection to the app and adds headers such as X-Forwarded-For.
The app server builds the response and sends it back to the proxy only, never to the browser directly.
If the response is cacheable the proxy saves it so the next visitor is served faster.
The proxy returns the response, and the browser never learns which server did the work.

title: How nginx picks a server and a location
summary: Two matching steps decide which block handles a request.

steps.n: The client sends a request whose Host header names the site it wants.
nginx compares the listening port and the Host header with each server block and selects the best match.
If nothing matches, the first or the default_server block answers, which is why unknown hosts reach a surprising site.
Inside the server, nginx tests exact locations, then the longest prefix, then regular expressions.
The chosen location sets root, proxy_pass or return rules, and only that block applies.
The result goes back to the client, and the access log records which location handled it.

title: What a proxy adds on the way to the app
summary: Headers carry the client identity that a proxy would otherwise hide.

steps.n: The client address 203.0.113.9 reaches the proxy, which is now the only peer the app can see.
The proxy sets X-Forwarded-For, X-Forwarded-Proto and Host so the app can know the original request.
The proxy buffers the response from the app so a slow client does not keep the app busy.
Without trusting the headers the app would log the proxy address for every user.
The app finishes quickly and is free for the next request while the proxy handles the slow client.
The proxy feeds the buffered response at the client's own speed.

title: TLS termination at the proxy
summary: The proxy ends encryption and talks plainly or re-encrypts to the app.

steps.n: The browser starts TLS and names the site it wants using the SNI extension.
The proxy picks the certificate that matches the name from its store.
The matching certificate and chain are loaded for the handshake.
Keys are agreed, HTTP/2 is negotiated and the browser sees a valid padlock.
The request travels encrypted to the proxy, which decrypts it.
The proxy forwards over a private network, optionally encrypting again for stricter environments.
The app answers and the proxy encrypts the reply for the browser.

title: Round robin with a health check
summary: The balancer stops sending traffic to a server that fails its check.

steps.n: The client request reaches the balancer, which picks the next server in rotation.
Server A is healthy so it receives the first request and answers it.
The next request arrives and the rotation moves on.
Server B takes the second request in the same way.
The balancer's periodic probe to B gets no answer for several tries in a row.
After the failure threshold B is removed from rotation without any human action.
A new request arrives while B is down.
All traffic now goes to A until B passes its probes again.

title: Timeout chain and a retry
summary: Every hop has its own timer and the shortest one wins.

steps.n: The client allows 60 seconds, the proxy read timeout is 30 seconds and the app has no limit of its own.
The proxy passes the request and starts its 30 second timer.
The app calls the database and the query runs longer than expected.
After 30 seconds the proxy gives up and prepares a 504 Gateway Timeout response.
The client receives an error while the app is still waiting for the database.
The app keeps working on a request nobody is waiting for, using a database connection.
If the proxy retried a non-idempotent request, the same order could be created twice.

title: Proxy cache hit and miss
summary: The first request fills the cache and later ones are served from it.

steps.n: A client asks for a product page that the proxy has not seen before.
The proxy builds a cache key from the URL and looks it up.
Nothing is stored for that key so the proxy must go to the app.
The app renders the page and returns it with Cache-Control headers.
The proxy writes the page to the cache with a lifetime taken from the headers.
Another client asks for the same page a moment later.
The cache returns the stored copy and the app is not touched.
The client receives the page in milliseconds with an X-Cache: HIT header.

title: A leaky bucket rate limit
summary: Requests above the rate are queued or rejected before they reach the app.

steps.n: A client sends 30 requests in one second against a limit of 10 per second.
The limiter counts requests for this client address in its shared memory zone.
The first requests within the rate and burst allowance continue to the proxy.
The app handles the allowed requests at a pace it can sustain.
Requests above the burst receive 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header.
A well-behaved client waits and retries later, so load smooths out.
When the client slows down the bucket drains and requests flow again.

title: HAProxy frontend to backend
summary: An ACL decides which backend serves a request.

steps.n: The frontend listens on port 443 and accepts the connection.
Rules test the request path, host name and headers, for example path_beg /api.
The first matching use_backend rule selects the api backend.
The backend balances across its servers with the configured algorithm and health checks.
The chosen server returns the response to HAProxy.
HAProxy sends the response back and records the timings in its log.

title: A dynamic proxy learns a new route
summary: New services appear without a restart or manual config edit.

steps.n: The orchestrator starts a new instance and registers it with discovery.
The control plane updates its model of routes and endpoints.
The new routes and endpoints are streamed to the proxy with no restart.
The proxy swaps in the new configuration and keeps existing connections alive.
Requests now match the new route and reach the new instance.
Health checks tell the proxy to remove the instance if it later fails.

title: A graceful reload
summary: New workers take new connections while old workers finish theirs.

steps.n: The operator edits the config and runs a syntax test, which must pass before anything else.
The operator sends a reload signal to the master process.
The master reads the new configuration and starts new workers with it.
Old workers stop accepting new connections but keep serving existing ones.
New connections go to the new workers using the new rules.
Old workers close once their last request is done, so no user sees an error.

title: Failure and recovery: 502 Bad Gateway after a deploy
summary: A restarted app is unreachable until it listens again.

steps.n: A user requests a page just after the app container restarts.
The proxy tries to connect to the app on its port.
The app process is not listening yet so the connection is refused.
The proxy returns 502 and logs connect() failed (111: Connection refused) while connecting to upstream.
The operator reads the proxy error log and sees the exact upstream address and error.
The operator finds the app is crash-looping because of a missing environment variable.
After restoring the variable the app listens again and passes its health check.
The proxy connects, requests succeed and the 502 count returns to zero.

title: Failure and recovery: 504 from a slow backend
summary: A slow dependency makes the proxy time out and retry.

steps.n: Requests increase during a sale and every one needs a slow database query.
The proxy forwards them and the app accepts more than the database can serve.
Queries queue up in the database and each response takes longer than 30 seconds.
The proxy timeout is reached and clients receive 504 errors.
Automatic retries send the same slow requests again, making the overload worse.
The team turns off retries, adds a rate limit and raises the database capacity.
With less load the queries finish in a few seconds and latency falls.
Responses arrive inside the timeout and the error rate returns to normal.
